question_text: Lithium reacts with water less vigorously than sodium. Give the reasons.

steps.label: Highest ionisation enthalpy
lines: Lithium has the smallest atom in
group 1, so its outer 2s electron is
Its ionisation enthalpy is therefore the
highest in the group, so the electron is
steps.why: The reaction with water starts with the metal giving up its outer electron. That electron is the most tightly held in lithium, so the first step of the reaction is slowest for lithium.
common_mistakes: Writing that lithium is the largest atom of group 1. It is the smallest, and atomic size increases down the group.
Saying lithium has a low ionisation enthalpy. Its ionisation enthalpy is the highest of the alkali metals, even though every alkali metal has the lowest value in its own period.
steps.memory_tip: Smallest atom, tightest hold on the outer electron, slowest start to the reaction.
steps.margin_note: Name the ionisation enthalpy, not just the small size.

steps.label: Strongest metallic bonding
lines: The small atom also gives lithium the
strongest metallic bonding, so it is
the hardest alkali metal and melts at
Sodium melts in the heat of its own
reaction and spreads out fresh metal,
while lithium stays solid, so lithium
reacts with water steadily and sodium
steps.why: How fast the reaction runs also depends on how much metal surface meets the water. Sodium melts and spreads, which keeps exposing new surface; lithium stays a solid piece, so its reacting surface stays small.
common_mistakes: Writing that lithium does not react with water. It does react, only more steadily than sodium.
Giving the melting points the wrong way round. Lithium melts at the highest temperature of the alkali metals.
steps.memory_tip: Sodium melts and spreads out; lithium stays a solid piece with a small surface.
steps.margin_note: Both reasons together: the tighter electron and the higher melting point.

insider_note: Lithium is the slowest alkali metal to react with water and is still the strongest reducing agent in aqueous solution, because reducing power in solution also depends on lithium's very large hydration enthalpy.
